Wind-direction instruments

Source: R/apx.R
windiv.Rd

Turns wind directions into indicators of the sector the wind blows from, one sector left out, optionally one set per area so that the same wind may act differently in different parts of a city; from hourly directions it first makes one per day.

Usage

windiv(
  dir,
  width = 90,
  start = 0,
  area = NULL,
  base = 1,
  sect = NULL,
  edges = c("halfopen", "paper"),
  by = NULL,
  avg = c("vector", "mode", "mean"),
  share = FALSE,
  spd = NULL
)

Arguments

dir

Wind directions in degrees (numbers; NA gives a row of NA, and is left out of a group's average).

width

The width of a sector in degrees; it must divide 360 into at most 67108864 (2^26) sectors.

start

Where the first sector begins, in degrees.

area

NULL or the area of each direction (labels; constant within a by group): one set of indicators per area, in sorted order of the labels.

base

The sector left out, counted from 1.

sect

NULL, or two numbers c(from, to) in degrees: then one indicator, 1 when the wind blows from between from (included) and to (excluded), going clockwise; width, start, base and edges are not used.

edges

"halfopen" or "paper".

by

NULL, or a group (day, or place and day) for each direction.

avg

"vector", "mode" or "mean": how a group's directions become one.

share

TRUE for the shares of each group's directions in each sector.

spd

NULL or wind speeds, weights of the vector average.

Value

A numeric matrix, one row per direction (or per by group, named by it), columns named "w<from>_<to>", with ":<area>" added when area is given. With by, the attribute "dir" holds the group's direction (for share, its vector average); a group whose winds cancel, or are calm, has no direction (NA) and no sector.

Details

The choices, and which paper made which:

Sectors (width, start, edges). Bondy, Roth and Sager (2020, footnote 18) use quadrants "0-90, 91-180, 181-270" degrees with the fourth left out, whole degrees closed at the top: edges = "paper". The default "halfopen" puts a boundary direction in the sector it opens, [lo, hi), which is the same for directions that are not whole numbers. Bondy, Roth and Sager let each of five regions of London have its own set (area), 15 instruments; their appendix also ranks four or eight directions by each ward's long-run pollution (table A3), which is not built here.

One sector (sect). Herrnstadt, Heyes, Muehlegger and Saberian (2019, footnote 24) use one indicator, wind from between 225 and 285 degrees (60 degrees); their table 5 widens it to 75 and 90 degrees without saying where the wider sectors start, so give sect as you choose it (for example c(217.5, 292.5) for 75 degrees about the same centre).

From hours to days (by, avg, share). With by, dir holds several directions per day (hours) and each group gives one row. avg = "vector" (the default) takes the direction of the mean wind vector, atan2(mean(sin), mean(cos)), weighted by spd when given: Herrnstadt and Muehlegger (2015, footnote 7) point out that 1 and 359 degrees average to north, not south. avg = "mode" takes the sector most hours fall in (ties: the first), the "predominant wind direction" of Bondy, Roth and Sager's figure A1. avg = "mean" is the plain mean of the angles, wrong across north and given only for comparison. share = TRUE instead gives the share of each group's hours in each sector, Bondy, Roth and Sager's instrument ("the share of hours in the 24 hours of each day", footnote 18); avg is then not used.

Other papers that use the indicators, and their choices. Karamik and von Graevenitz (2022, sec. 3.1) cut the circle into four 90-degree bins, "North-East is equivalent to [0 till 90)", with "the South-West ... the most common wind direction in Germany" left out (width = 90, base = 3), the direction averaged per region and day and allowed to act differently in each region (area; their robustness check narrows the bins to 60 degrees). Batkeyev and DeRemer (2023, sec. 4.3) use "the [0,1] share of weather observations within each time period for which winds are blowing from the southeast, south-by-southeast, or east-by-southeast", the three 22.5-degree points from 101.25 to 168.75 degrees (sect = c(101.25, 168.75), by the period, share = TRUE), for the city's five southern districts and 0 for the northern ones. Singh and Visaria (2021, eq 4) assign each police station the wind of the nearest grid point and use "eight wind direction bins ... based on the octant from which the wind blows", interacted with the nine administrative divisions of Bihar, with "wind from the east as the base" (63 instruments); with octants centred on the compass points that is width = 45, start = 22.5, base = 2 and area the division (the paper does not say where its octants start). Sarmiento (2020, eqs 7-8) enters "wind direction" in an hourly station-level first stage without saying in what form; the sectors here are one form, and the choice should be reported.

Directions are where the wind blows from, in degrees clockwise from north; 360 is 0. The indicators are instruments only if the wind direction affects the outcome through the exposure alone (see ivfe()).

References

Bondy, M., Roth, S. and Sager, L. (2020). Crime is in the air: the contemporaneous relationship between air pollution and crime. Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists, 7(3), 555-585. doi:10.1086/707127

Herrnstadt, E., Heyes, A., Muehlegger, E. and Saberian, S. (2019). Air pollution as a cause of violent crime. Working paper.

Herrnstadt, E. and Muehlegger, E. (2015). Air pollution and criminal activity: evidence from Chicago microdata. NBER Working Paper 21787. doi:10.3386/w21787

Karamik, Y. and von Graevenitz, K. (2022). Gone with the wind: the effect of air pollution on crime. Evidence from Germany. ZEW Mannheim working paper. doi:10.2139/ssrn.4130091

Batkeyev, B. and DeRemer, D. R. (2023). Mountains of evidence: the effects of abnormal air pollution on crime. Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization, 210, 288-319. doi:10.1016/j.jebo.2023.04.009

Sarmiento, L. (2020). I am innocent: hourly variations in air pollution and crime behavior. DIW Berlin Discussion Paper. doi:10.2139/ssrn.3639084

Singh, T. P. and Visaria, S. (2021). Up in the air: air pollution and crime. Evidence from India. Working paper, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

See also

ivfe(), ppmlcf(), invsn(), dwnexp()

Examples

windiv(c(10, 100, 200, 300))
#>      w90_180 w180_270 w270_0
#> [1,]       0        0      0
#> [2,]       1        0      0
#> [3,]       0        1      0
#> [4,]       0        0      1
# the paper's whole-degree quadrants: 90 is in the first
windiv(c(90, 91), edges = "paper")
#>      w90_180 w180_270 w270_0
#> [1,]       0        0      0
#> [2,]       1        0      0
# quadrants by region, as in London
windiv(c(10, 100, 200, 300), area = c("east", "east", "west", "west"))
#>      w90_180:east w180_270:east w270_0:east w90_180:west w180_270:west
#> [1,]            0             0           0            0             0
#> [2,]            1             0           0            0             0
#> [3,]            0             0           0            0             1
#> [4,]            0             0           0            0             0
#>      w270_0:west
#> [1,]           0
#> [2,]           0
#> [3,]           0
#> [4,]           1
# one westerly sector
windiv(c(230, 300), sect = c(225, 285))
#>      w225_285
#> [1,]        1
#> [2,]        0
# hours to days: 350 and 10 degrees average to north
windiv(c(350, 10, 100, 120), by = c(1, 1, 2, 2))
#>   w90_180 w180_270 w270_0
#> 1       0        0      0
#> 2       1        0      0
#> attr(,"dir")
#> [1] 360 110
windiv(c(350, 10, 100, 120), by = c(1, 1, 2, 2), share = TRUE)
#>   w90_180 w180_270 w270_0
#> 1       0        0    0.5
#> 2       1        0    0.0
#> attr(,"dir")
#> [1] 360 110
